gapFill.title: Fill in the gaps
gapFill.subtitle: 20 original sentences covering all three forms (affirmative, negative, question) and the three uses from the lesson: experience, present result, and a situation that continues — always the simple form, never the continuous.

questions.explain: An experience at an unspecified time — we don't say exactly when it happened.

questions.after: my keys — I can't find them anywhere.
questions.explain: A finished action with a result now: that's why you can't find your keys.
'Know' is a stative verb — always simple, never continuous. 'Since' marks the starting point.
Negative with 'yet': the results haven't arrived.
A question about experience: 'ever' + present perfect.
'Just' signals a very recent action, relevant right now.
'Have' as a stative verb (to own) — never continuous, even with 'for' + a period.

questions.after: in a hot air balloon once.
questions.explain: A one-time experience — 'once' doesn't say exactly when.

questions.after: this book yet — no spoilers, please!
questions.explain: Negative with 'yet'.
'Already' — the action is complete, with an effect now.

questions.after: classical music since she was a child.
questions.explain: 'Love' is a stative verb — it isn't used in the continuous form.
A question about a recent fact, with 'yet'.

questions.after: this film before — let's watch something else.
questions.explain: 'Before' with no specific time — an experience.
'Yet' in a negative: she hasn't told anyone up to now — present perfect.
'Own' is a stative verb — never continuous, even with 'for' + a period.

questions.after: her homework — she can go out now.
questions.explain: The result is visible now: that's why she can go out.

questions.after: she ever been to New York?
questions.explain: A question about experience with 'been' — 'has' for the third person.

questions.after: in ghosts since he was a child.
questions.explain: 'Believe' is a stative verb — never continuous.
'Never' + present perfect — a negative experience.
A question about a result now, with 'yet' — 'have' with 'you'.

wordOrder.title: Put the words in order
wordOrder.subtitle: Tap the words below to build each sentence in the right order. Twenty original sentences, mixing statements, negatives and questions — all present perfect simple.

matching.title: Match the past participles
matching.subtitle: Tap a base verb, then tap its irregular past participle. Present perfect always needs the participle, never the base form — these twenty are the ones learners mix up most.

timedMC.title: Beat the clock
timedMC.subtitle: 15 seconds per question. Pick the option that completes the sentence correctly — the auxiliary, the participle, and the tense all have to be right.

questions.text: Have you ever        a famous person?
wrongReasons: Missing participle: after "have", use the past participle — "met", not the base form.
Wrong tense: with "ever", this needs the present perfect (have + past participle), not the simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "you", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
questions.explain: Experience up to now, with no specific time — present perfect.

questions.text: Someone        my bike. I'll have to walk.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: the simple past doesn't show the present result ("I'll have to walk now") — use present perfect.
Subject-verb agreement: "someone" is singular, so the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
Wrong participle: after "has", use the past participle — "stolen", not "stole".
questions.explain: A past action with a visible result right now — present perfect.

questions.text: We        friends since primary school.
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: with "we", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong tense: "since" needs present perfect here, not the present simple.
Wrong tense: the simple past doesn't connect the friendship to now — with "since", use present perfect.
questions.explain: A state that started in the past and is still true now, with "since" — present perfect.

questions.text: They        the new bridge yet.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: in British English, "yet" signals present perfect, not simple past.
Missing participle: after "haven't", use the past participle — "built".
Subject-verb agreement: with "they", the auxiliary is "haven't", not "hasn't".
questions.explain: Something expected that hasn't happened up to now, with "yet" — present perfect negative.

questions.text: she started her new job?
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: with "she", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
Wrong tense: "started" here is a participle, so the question needs "Has", not "Did".
Wrong auxiliary: present perfect questions use "have"/"has", not "is".
questions.explain: A yes/no question about whether a result exists now — present perfect.

questions.text: I        that song a hundred times so far.
wrongReasons: Missing participle: after "have", use the past participle — "heard", not "hear".
Wrong tense: "so far" counts experiences up to now — that needs present perfect, not simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "I", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
questions.explain: Counting how many times something has happened up to now — present perfect.

questions.text: He        as a nurse for ten years, and he still loves it.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: he still works as a nurse, so "for ten years" up to now needs present perfect, not simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "he", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
Missing participle: after "has", use the past participle — "worked", not "work".
questions.explain: A situation that started in the past and continues now, with "for" — present perfect.

questions.text: you watered the plants?
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: "watered" here is a participle — the question needs "Have you watered", not the simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "you", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong auxiliary: present perfect questions use "have"/"has", not "was".
questions.explain: A yes/no question about whether a result exists now — present perfect.

questions.text: I        never been to Japan.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: "never" with an experience up to now needs present perfect, not simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "I", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong auxiliary: present perfect uses "have"/"has", not "was".
questions.explain: Experience up to now (or the lack of it) — present perfect.

questions.text: Prices        since 2020.
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: "prices" is plural, so the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong tense: "since 2020" needs present perfect, not simple past.
Missing participle: after "have", use the past participle — "doubled", not "double".
questions.explain: A change that started in the past and is still relevant now, with "since" — present perfect.

questions.text: He        that marathon four times so far.
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: with "he", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
Wrong tense: "so far" counts experiences up to now — that needs present perfect, not simple past.
Wrong participle: after "has", use the past participle — "run", not "ran".
questions.explain: Counting how many times something has happened up to now — present perfect.

questions.text: I        my glasses. I can't see properly.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: the simple past doesn't show the present result ("I can't see now") — use present perfect.
Missing participle: after "have", use the past participle — "broken", not "break".
Subject-verb agreement: with "I", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
questions.explain: A past action with a visible result right now — present perfect.

questions.text: Many scientists        this theory for decades, and they still do.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: they still believe it, so "for decades" up to now needs present perfect, not simple past.
Missing participle: after "have", use the past participle — "believed", not "believe".
Subject-verb agreement: "scientists" is plural, so the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
questions.explain: A state that started in the past and continues now, with "for" — present perfect.

questions.text: He        the dishes yet.
wrongReasons: Missing participle: after "hasn't", use the past participle — "washed".
Wrong tense: in British English, "yet" signals present perfect, not simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "he", the auxiliary is "hasn't", not "haven't".
questions.explain: Something expected that hasn't happened up to now, with "yet" — present perfect negative.

questions.text: you ever seen a ghost?
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: "ever" asks about experience up to now, so it needs "Have you ever seen", not the simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "you", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong auxiliary: present perfect questions use "have"/"has", not "was".
questions.explain: Experience up to now, with no specific time — present perfect.

questions.text: The printer        . I can't print my essay.
wrongReasons: Missing participle: after "has", use the past participle — "broken", not "break".
Wrong tense: the simple past doesn't show the present result ("I can't print now") — use present perfect.
Subject-verb agreement: with "the printer", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
questions.explain: A past action with a visible result right now — present perfect.

questions.text: My grandparents        that sofa since 1990.
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: "my grandparents" is plural, so the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong tense: "since 1990" up to now needs present perfect, not simple past.
Wrong participle: after "have", use the past participle — "had", not "have" again.
questions.explain: A state that started in the past and continues now, with "since" — present perfect.

questions.text: they sold their house yet?
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: in British English, "yet" asks about a result now, so it needs "Have they sold", not the simple past.
Subject-verb agreement: with "they", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
Wrong auxiliary: present perfect questions use "have"/"has", not "were".
questions.explain: A yes/no question about whether a result exists now — present perfect.

questions.text: We        never seen such a beautiful sunset.
wrongReasons: Wrong tense: "never" with an experience up to now needs present perfect, not simple past — and "did" can't go with "seen".
Wrong auxiliary: present perfect uses "have"/"has", not "were".
Subject-verb agreement: with "we", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
questions.explain: Experience up to now (or the lack of it) — present perfect.

questions.text: The company        its prices twice this year.
wrongReasons: Subject-verb agreement: with "the company", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
Wrong tense: "twice this year" counts events up to now — that needs present perfect, not simple past.
Missing participle: after "has", use the past participle — "raised", not "raise".
questions.explain: Counting how many times something has happened up to now — present perfect.

errorCorrection.title: Find the mistake
errorCorrection.subtitle: Each sentence has exactly one mistake. Tap the word you think is wrong. Twenty original sentences.

items.message: With "she", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
After "have", use the past participle — "worn", not "wore" (that's the simple past form).
With "they", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
With "he", the auxiliary is "hasn't", not "haven't".
After "have", use the past participle — "sung", not "sang" (that's the simple past form).
After "have", use the past participle — "swum", not "swam" (that's the simple past form).
After "have", use the past participle — "cleaned", not the base form "clean".
After "has", use the past participle — "forgotten", not "forgot" (that's the simple past form).
After "has", use the past participle — "gone", not "went" (that's the simple past form).
After "haven't", use the past participle — "eaten", not "ate" (that's the simple past form).
After "have", use the past participle — "written", not "wrote" (that's the simple past form).
With "my dad", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
With "we", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
With "he", the auxiliary is "has", not "have".
With "I", the auxiliary is "have", not "has".
In British English, "already" needs the present perfect — "have sent", not the simple past alone.
"Since nine o'clock" up to now needs the present perfect — "have been", not the present simple.
"Since Monday" needs the present perfect — "have known", not the simple past.
In British English, "yet" signals the present perfect negative — "hasn't packed", not "didn't pack".
This mixes the simple past auxiliary ("did") with a present perfect participle ("climbed"). Use "Have you ever climbed" instead.

Negative with 'yet': the decision hasn't happened up to now.

items.sentText: She {{blank}} allergic to cats since she was a baby.
items.explain: 'Be' is a stative verb: a state that started in the past and is still true now, with "since" — present perfect.
An experience at an unspecified time — we don't say exactly when it happened.

wrongReasons: Wrong form: "grew" is the simple past, not the participle.
There's no such form as "growed" — irregular verbs don't take -ed.
"Growing" is the -ing form, not the participle.
items.explain: 'Grow' is irregular: grow → grew → grown. The participle is 'grown'.

wrongReasons: Wrong form: "fell" is the simple past, not the participle.
There's no such form as "falled" — "fall" is irregular.
"Falling" is the -ing form, not the participle.
items.explain: 'Fall' is irregular: fall → fell → fallen. The participle is 'fallen'.

wrongReasons: Wrong form: "threw" is the simple past, not the participle.
There's no such form as "throwed" — "throw" is irregular.
"Throwing" is the -ing form, not the participle.
items.explain: 'Throw' is irregular: throw → threw → thrown. The participle is 'thrown'.

items.text: I have {{blank}} all my coffee — the cup is empty.
wrongReasons: Wrong form: "drank" is the simple past, not the participle.
There's no such form as "drinked" — "drink" is irregular.
"Drinking" is the -ing form, not the participle.
items.explain: 'Drink' is irregular: drink → drank → drunk. The participle is 'drunk'.
